J U D G M E N T
1. Leave granted.
2. The question for our consideration is whether fee payable for
professional education through self-financing Higher Education
Institutions (HEIs) can be changed midstream. While we uphold the
decision of the division bench of the High Court,
1 that the fees determined
at the commencement of the course cannot be varied midstream, for the
independent and separate reasons to follow, we have held that
determination of the fee payable for professional education such as
medicine, engineering, pharmacy etc. conducted by professional HEIs
involves balancing of two legitimate interests. Firstly, the interest of
students and their parents in fixation of a reasonable fee, as also the
certainty about the quantum and the time. Secondly, the interest of self-financing HEIs in securing adequate resources for developing necessary
infrastructure and provide quality education. Pursuant to the judgments of
this Court in TMA Pai Foundation and Others v. State of Karnataka and
Others,
2 and P.A. Inamdar and Others v. State of Maharashtra and
Others,
3 fee fixation committees constituted for determining the
appropriate fee payable must be given institutional status. They are
1 Common judgment and order dated 23.03.2026 passed by the Calcutta High Court in MAT No. 268
of 2026, FMA No. 284 of 2026, and FMA No. 288 of 2026, reported as Tanushri Mondal and Others v
State of West Bengal and Others, 2026 SCC OnLine Cal 2382.
2 (2002) 8 SCC 481. 3 (2005) 6 SCC 537.

3
virtually the regulatory bodies for determining the appropriate fee and
must therefore perform their duties with efficiency, expertise and integrity.
As they perform an important public function, their actions are subject to
review.
Facts
3. The West Bengal Joint Entrance Examinations ('WBJEE') 2023 was
conducted on 30.04.2023 for admissions to engineering colleges in West
Bengal with respect to courses commencing from the 2023-24 Academic
Year ('AY'). WBJEE results were declared on 26.05.2023. Parallelly,
results of the Joint Entrance Examination (Main) ('JEE (Main)') were also
declared, and candidates were ranked in order of merit with respect to
both examinations, with both sets of scores and ranks for admission to
engineering colleges under the counselling process.
4. The West Bengal Joint Entrance Examinations Board, a statutory
body, conducted the WBJEE Centralised Counselling between July-August 2023. After conclusion of the counselling process, candidates
reported to their allocated colleges, had their documents verified, and,
upon deposit of fees, their admission processes were concluded. In
September 2023, the Respondents-Students were admitted as students
of Bachelor of Technology ('B.Tech.') courses, for the 2023-27 cohort, at
the Dr. B.C. Roy Engineering College ('the Appellant-College'), a self-

4
financing college affiliated to the Maulana Abul Kalam Azad University of
Technology.
5. It is important to note that the prospectus of the Appellant-College
had a specific clause stating that, "fee structure is subject to change from
time to time as per Government decision." The following is a simplified
version of the per-semester fee structure that was applicable to students
who had joined the 2023-27 cohort:

5
6. About one-and-a-half months after admissions closed, the
Department of Higher Education, Government of West Bengal issued a
Notification dated 16.10.2023 revising the upper ceiling of fees chargeable
by self-financing professional colleges, such as the Appellant-College,
allowing them to enhance their fees to a maximum of ₹1,10,000/- per
annum per student. The Notification made this new arrangement
applicable from the 2023-24 AY itself. The text of the Notification is
reproduced hereinbelow for ready reference:
"No. 466-Edn-(T)/10M-04/2004 (Part IV) Date: 16.10.2023
NOTIFICATION
Regarding the fees of Under Graduate Engineering &
Technology, Pharmacy and Architecture Programmes
conducted by the Private Self-financing Engineering &
Technology, Pharmacy and Architecture Colleges of this State,
the Governor is pleased to order that the Fees Structure for the
Programmes conducted by the Private Self-financing
Engineering & Technology, Pharmacy and Architecture Colleges
of this State will be continued for at least four (04) years for B.
Tech and B. Pharm courses and five (05) years for B. Arch
courses w.e.f. 2023-2024 academic session.
Now, the details of Fees Structure stipulated in 2023-24
academic year are enumerated in this order.
Accordingly, the Tuition fees and other fees for the students
to be admitted in the 1st year of under Graduate Engineering &
Technology, Pharmacy and Architecture Courses and Students
admitted through lateral entry in the Self-financing Engineering
& Technology, Pharmacy and Architecture Colleges in the State
with effect from the academic year 2023-2024 are given here
under:-
I) Maximum Annual Tuition Fee will be Rs. 1,10,000/- per
annum per Student.

6
II) In addition to the prescribed tuition fees, Institutes may
charge development fees not exceeding 15% of the
prescribed tuition fees for future expansion and development
of the Institute.
III) Besides Tuition Fees as prescribed above, the Self-financing Colleges may charge the following fees from the
students admitted with effect from the academic year 2023-
2024.
a) Maximum onetime Admission Fee of Rs. 10,000/- for
entire Course period.
b) Library-cum-Book-Bank Fee not exceeding Rs. 6,000/-
for the entire course period.
c) Students Welfare, Sports & Games Fee not exceeding
Rs. 1,000/- annually.
d) A reasonable amount as Refundable Caution Money.
e) Fees charged by the University for Welfare of students
and Development.
f) Other usual University Fees like Registration Fee,
Examination Fee, etc.
IV) Professional Colleges which have obtained Autonomous
Status, have earned NBA accreditation (Program
wise)/NAAC/NIRF ranking from the National level Regulatory
Authority/Authorities at the time of their admission process
can charge a maximum 10% additional tuition fees above the
prescribed maximum fees for the said Programme(s). Such
additional fees can be charged from the students for entire
duration of the Program.
V) Colleges have to implement the West Bengal Freeship
Scheme (WBFS) as per the Govt. Order issued from time to
time in this regard.
VI) No capitation fee in any form or kind can be demanded or
realized from the students for admission or continuation of the
study in the colleges or for any other reason, either directly or
indirectly.
VII) No college shall demand or charge any other fee of
compulsory nature except fees prescribed in the Para-I to IV
of this Order.
VIII) In case of any violation or deviation from any condition of
this order, the State Government shall take appropriate action.
IX) The Private Self Financing Engineering &
Technology/Pharmacy/Architecture colleges shall submit the
college specific audited annual accounts and annual
administrative reports to the Registrar of the affiliating
University and the Director of Technical Education at the
earliest.

7
X) The Affiliating University MAKAUT will conduct and
evaluate Academic Audit and Performance to ensure that the
desired quality of education is available in and provided by the
said self financing colleges and will submit report to the State
Government at a regular interval for the purpose of suitable
Ranking System for self financing Engineering &
Technology/Pharmacy/Architecture colleges in the State.
This Notification is issued with the approval of the
Competent Authority in the Higher Education Department and in
supersession of all previous orders and/or Notifications issued
by this Department on this subject and will take effect from the
date of notification."
7. The genesis of this 2023 Notification lay in a belated fee revision
exercise, with the delay being the reason for the entire controversy.
8. On 15.11.2019, the State Government had constituted an Expert
Committee to assess and make recommendations on fees payable by
students for undergraduate professional courses in West Bengal. The
Expert Committee had consulted a range of stakeholders, including self-financing professional colleges, and recommended that the upper ceiling
of fees chargeable be enhanced. The Expert Committee's
recommendation was considered and adopted by the Fee Structure
Committee on 09.06.2023 and forwarded to the State Government for
necessary action. Thus, after a hiatus of seven years since the last fee
revision exercise, the Notification was issued in 2023 and a new fee
arrangement for self-financing professional colleges put in place.
9. Pursuant to the Notification, the Appellant-College, on 15.12.2023,
i.e., after classes for the semester were well underway, revised the fee
structure for the 2023-27 cohort, raising the per semester tuition fee. In

8
addition to this upward revision of the tuition fee, the Appellant-College
also imposed a new "development fee", payable by each student on a per
semester basis. The revised fee structure was made applicable from
January 2024, i.e., second semester onwards. The resultant impact of the
revised structure was a 37.5% increase in the fees payable by each
student. A simplified version of the revised fee structure is presented in
the following table:

9
10. Aggrieved by this fee hike during the 2023-24 AY, students made
representations to the Appellant-College seeking a rollback of the revised
fee structure. When the Appellant-College did not accede to this demand,
the students filed writ petitions before the Calcutta High Court challenging
the Notification and the Appellant-College's revised fee structure.4 During
the course of the writ proceedings, the students abandoned their
challenge to the Notification and confined their contest to the legality and
validity of applying the revised fee structure to students admitted in the
2023-24 AY for the 2023-27 courses.
11. Before the High Court, the students' principal contention was that
the Appellant-College's upward fee revision was in violation of Regulation
7 of the All India Council for Technical Education (Norms and Guidelines
for Fees and Guidelines for Admission in Professional Colleges)
Regulations, 1994 ('AICTE Regulations 1994'). Regulation 7 reads as
follows:
"Regulation 7. Fee. - (1) Tuition and other fees for professional
college shall be determined by a State Level committee.
(2) The Council shall constitute a standing committee for each
State to fix ceiling on the fees chargeable for individual courses
by a professional college or class of professional colleges, as
the case may be. The Standing committee shall consist of the
following members namely:-
(i) Vice-Chancellor of a University in a State, to be
nominated by the State Government.
(ii) Secretaries, Department of Technical Education and
Department of Finance of the respective State, ex-officio.
4 WPA Nos. 13054, 26400, and 3028 of 2024.

10
(iii) Two economists or experts in cost accountancy with
background of institutional financing, to be nominated by
the Council.
(iv) Member-Secretary not below the rank of Joint
Secretary or Director of the respective State Government,
to be nominated by the State Government.
(3) The members referred to in clauses (i), (iii), (iv) shall hold
office for a period of three years from the date of their
nomination.
(4) The Committee shall give an opportunity to the professional
colleges to place such material, as they think relevant in
determining the tuition fee and other fees. The fee shall be fixed
once in every three years or at such longer intervals, as the
Committee may think appropriate.
(5) The fees chargeable in professional colleges shall be
determined on the basis of estimation of expenditure of the
professional college for its efficient function. The committee
shall take the items specified in the Annexure to these
regulations, into account while determining the tuition fee and
other fees to be charged by a professional college. The
committee may in its directions take into consideration a
reasonable return on capital investment with reference to the
investment made and determine the fees accordingly. While
calculating the fees, the estimates of recurring expenditure shall
be based on at least the last two years audited figures of
recurring expenditure of the college and projected requirement
for next three years.
(6) No professional college shall be entitled to receive from the
student any other payment or amount, or whatever name it may
be called in addition to the fee fixed by the committee for a free
seat or payment seat.
(7) A professional college shall send intimation to the competent
authority in advance the fees chargeable for the entire course
commencing from the academic year for which admissions shall
be made. The total fees shall be divided into the number of
years, or as the case may be, the number of semesters of study
for a course. In the first instance, fees only for the first year or
semester shall be collected. The fee chargeable by a
Professional College shall be subject to the ceiling fixed by the
Standing committee."
(emphasis supplied)

11
12. Proceedings before the High Court: The Learned Single Judge,
by his judgment dated 15.01.2026,5 dismissed the writ petitions, holding
that neither the Notification approving upward revision of the fees for the
4-year B.Tech and B.Pharm courses commencing from 2023-24 AY nor
Regulation 7(7) of the AICTE Regulations 1994 treated the fee structure
as indivisible. Referring to the explicit clause of the Appellant-College's
prospectus prescribing that "fee structure is subject to change from time
to time as per Government decision", the Learned Single Judge held that
there was no legal infirmity in the revision of the Appellant-College's fee
structure. While dismissing the writ petitions, the Learned Single Judge
also held that writ jurisdiction cannot be invoked to avoid a contractual
obligation.
13. Aggrieved, the students filed writ appeals before a Division Bench
of the Calcutta High Court.
14. The Division Bench formulated three issues: (i) whether Regulation
7(7) of the AICTE Regulations 1994 was violated by the Notification, (ii)
the purport of the Appellant-College's original fee structure, and (iii)
whether the Notification was applicable to already admitted students.
15. Differing with the conclusions drawn by the Learned Single Judge,
the Division Bench accepted the students' submission that Regulation
5 Reported as Gourab Kumar Sadhu and Others v State of West Bengal and Others, 2026 SCC OnLine
Cal 390.

12
7(7) contemplated an en bloc fixation of fees for the entire course. Further,
interpreting the language of the Appellant-College's original fee structure,
it concluded that the fee arrangement was intended to continue for the full
duration of the 2023-27 courses. With respect to the applicability of the
revised fee structure under the Notification, the Division Bench held that
it would be applicable to students admitted on or after 16.10.2023 and
those of subsequent batches, e.g., the 2024-28 cohort. The Division
Bench was of the view that applying the revised fee structure to already-admitted students would give the Notification retrospective effect contrary
to its explicit text. It further invoked the doctrines of equity and estoppel
as the students had relied on the fee information made available by the
Appellant-College at the time of admission. Finally, while applying the
revised fee schedule vis-à-vis students admitted after 16.10.2023, the
Division Bench further directed a refund of the enhanced fee collected
from students admitted prior to that date. The relevant portion of the
Impugned Judgment is as follows:
"75. Accordingly, MAT No. 268 of 2026, FMA No. 284 of 2026
and FMA No. 288 of 2026 are partially allowed on contest,
thereby setting aside the impugned judgments dated January
15, 2026, passed in WPA No. 26400 of 2024, WPA No. 13054
of 2024 and WPA No. 3028 of 2024 respectively, with the
following findings/directions:
(I) The impugned Notification, bearing no. 466-Edn-
(T)/10M-04/2004 (Part IV) dated October 16, 2023, is read
down to be applicable for the academic year 2023-24
onwards, at least for four years in respect of B.Tech and B.
Pharm courses and five years for B.Arch. courses, only in
respect of students who were admitted or shall be admitted

13
on and from October 16, 2023 onwards. However, the
impugned Notification shall not apply to students whose
admission process for the academic session 2023-2027,
starting from the academic year 2023-2024, stood
completed before October 16, 2023.
(II) The revised fee structures published in terms of the
impugned Notification dated October 16, 2023 by the
respondent no. 10-College and all other colleges coming
under the umbrella of the said Notification are hereby
quashed and set aside to the limited extent insofar as those
apply to the students of such colleges whose admission
process stood concluded before October 16, 2023 and
shall be applicable only to those students who were or shall
be admitted on and from October 16, 2023.
(III) Any action taken in terms of the impugned Notification
shall stand reversed, insofar as the candidates whose
admission process stood concluded before October 16,
2023 are concerned.
(IV) Additional amounts, if any, collected from any such
student (whose admission process stood concluded before
October 16, 2023) in terms of revised fee structures framed
pursuant to the impugned Notification dated October 16,
2023, shall be refunded by the respondent no. 10-college
and all other colleges standing on similar footing to the
respective students who have paid such additional
amounts, before commencement of the next semester.
(V) Alternatively, such additional amount shall be adjusted
with the fees payable by the aforementioned students
(whose admission process stood concluded before
October 16, 2023) for the next semester in terms of the fee
structure prevailing prior to the impugned Notification; in
the event, even after such adjustment with the next
semester fees, a part of the additional amounts paid by
such students still remains unrefunded, such balance
amounts shall be refunded by the concerned colleges to
the concerned students within one month from the
commencement of such next semester."
16. Aggrieved by the judgment of the Division Bench, the Appellant-College and other self-financing professional colleges, represented by the
Association of Professional Academic Institutes, West Bengal, are in
appeal before us.

14
17. We have heard Mr. Jaideep Gupta, Mr. Harin Raval, and Mr. Rauf
Rahim, learned Senior Advocates for the Appellants, and Mr. Sanjay R.
Hegde, learned Senior Advocate for the Respondents.
Analysis
18. The determination of fees payable for professional education
imparted through self-financing higher educational institutions involves
three legitimate interests which must coordinate and operate together.
The first is the interest of students and parents in certainty and
predictability about the reasonable fee payable for the course. The second
is the interest of self-financing educational institutions in securing
adequate resources for providing quality education and also for the future
development of the institution. The third is the societal interest,
represented by the fee fixation committees and the concerned
government, to ensure fixation of reasonable and appropriate fee, and
also the appropriate timeframe for effective and efficient implementation.
Interests of Students and Teachers
19. An empirical study based on data collected by the National
Statistical Office ('NSO') examining the socio-economic and institutional

15
factors determining household expenditure on professional higher
education in India6 suggested that:
"The annual average household expenditure on higher
education in India is Rs.26,400, which accounts for 17.3%
of the total annual household consumption expenditure in
2017-2018. Fees accounted for 61.2%, and non-fee
spending constituted 38.8% of the overall spending.
Although this is the picture for overall higher education, we
notice a significant difference in household spending
between general and professional courses. Students
pursing professional courses spent remarkably higher on
their education (483% more) than those attending general
courses. Households spend around 46.7% and 9.7% of
their annual consumption expenditure if one of their children
is pursuing a professional course and general course,
respectively, marking a huge difference. This is largely due
to higher fees charged (particularly in private institutions) in
professional courses such as engineering, management,
medicine and law. Estimates reveal that the fee charged in
professional courses is reported to be 711% more than in
general courses."7
Thus, the aforesaid study reveals that students pursuing professional
courses spend remarkably higher amount on their education and the
estimates reveal that fee charged in professional courses is reported to
be 711% more than the general courses.
20. For the overwhelming majority of households, the fee payable for a
professional course constitutes a substantial part of the family's income
and savings; it is not a matter of incidental expenditure. The parents make
6 Pradeep Kumar Choudhury and Amit Kumar, 'How Much do Households Spend on Professional
Higher Education in India? Results from a National Survey' (2022) 16(1) Indian Journal of Human
Development 77.
7 ibid 83.

16
the provision for payment of fee payable for the professional courses with
the aspiration that their children will acquire better qualifications, secure
better opportunities, and build a future that may be better than their own.
Many students and families also depend on educational loans to finance
professional higher education.
21. It is a matter of good governance for the state and its regulatory
bodies to create an ecosystem in which there is certainty about the
financial obligation that students and their families need to undertake for
acquiring professional qualifications. Adverse variations in financial
commitment, and the insecurities that it may create, will impact the student
and the family, and, in the long run, have an adverse effect on the quality
and character of the professionals that are in the making. We are of the
opinion that it is not difficult to formulate a scheme through which such
uncertainties can be avoided.
Participation of Private Enterprise in Nation Building and the Need
to Secure Their Interests
22. Our nation's demand for high-quality professional education cannot
realistically be sustained exclusively through public resources. In this
backdrop, private enterprise contributes meaningfully in building our
nation's higher educational system. The role of such private enterprise in

17
higher educational institutions is recognised in TMA Pai Foundation and
Others v. State of Karnataka and Others,
8 wherein this Court held
"48. Private education is one of the most dynamic and
fastest-growing segments of post-secondary education at
the turn of the twenty-first century. A combination of
unprecedented demand for access to higher education and
the inability or unwillingness of the Government to provide
the necessary support has brought private higher education
to the forefront. Private institutions, with a long history in
many countries, are expanding in scope and number, and
are becoming increasingly important in parts of the world
that relied almost entirely on the public sector.
49. Not only has demand overwhelmed the ability of the
Governments to provide education, there has also been a
significant change in the way that higher education is
perceived. The idea of an academic degree as a "private
good" that benefits the individual rather than a "public good"
for society is now widely accepted. The logic of today's
economics and an ideology of privatization have contributed
to the resurgence of private higher education, and the
establishing of private institutions where none or very few
existed before."
23. This Court also recognised the role of private unaided professional
colleges and held as follows:
"70. It is well established all over the world that those who
seek professional education must pay for it. The number of
seats available in government and government-aided
colleges is very small, compared to the number of persons
seeking admission to the medical and engineering colleges.
All those eligible and deserving candidates who could not
be accommodated in government colleges would stand
deprived of professional education. This void in the field of
medical and technical education has been filled by
institutions that are established in different places with the
aid of donations and the active part taken by public-minded
individuals. The object of establishing an institution has thus
been to provide technical or professional education to the
8 (2002) 8 SCC 481.

18
deserving candidates, and is not necessarily a commercial
venture. In order that this intention is meaningful, the
institution must be recognized..... A college or a
professional educational institution has to get recognition
from the university concerned, which normally requires
certain conditions to be fulfilled before recognition..."
24. Self-financing institutions necessarily require substantial
investment in land, buildings, facilities, student services, libraries,
equipment, technology, and the like. They must be capable of drawing
and retaining competent teaching faculty and other professional staff by
providing them suitable, if not attractive, remuneration. After meeting
legitimate operational and developmental expenditure, the institutions
must also be permitted a reasonable return for sustenance and further
development.
The Institutional Mechanism for Balancing the Interests of Students
and Educational Institutions
25. In pursuance of the judgment of this Court in TMA Pai Foundation
(supra) and subsequent decisions,
9 a regulatory mechanism has been
evolved, as the State Legislatures have enacted laws and the State
Governments have constituted regulatory committees to establish an
objective mechanism for fixation of fees payable by the students. A
regulatory framework relevant for the purposes of the controversy
9 Islamic Academy of Education and Another v. State of Karnataka and Others, (2003) 6 SCC 697; P.A.
Inamdar and Others v. State of Maharashtra and Others, (2005) 6 SCC 537.

19
involved in these appeals is contained in the provisions of AICTE
Regulations, 1994 and National Education Policy ('NEP-2020'). The said
regulatory framework operates to pre-empt arbitrary increases in the fee
by self-financing higher educational institutions while preserving
legitimate fiscal space for self-financing institutions. NEP-2020 also
envisions empowering private/self-financing higher educational
institutions to set the fees for their programmes through a fair regulatory
mechanism. The relevant extract of the NEP-2020 reads as under:
"18.13. All HEIs - public and private - shall be treated on par
within this regulatory regime. The regulatory regime shall
encourage private philanthropic efforts in education. There
will be common national guidelines for all legislative Acts
that will form private HEIs. These common minimal
guidelines will enable all such Acts to establish private HEIs,
thus enabling common standards for private and public
HEIs. These common guidelines will cover Good
Governance, Financial Stability & Security, Educational
Outcomes, and Transparency of Disclosures.
18.14. Private HEIs having a philanthropic and public-spirited intent will be encouraged through a progressive
regime of fees determination. Transparent mechanisms for
fixing of fees with an upper limit, for different types of
institutions depending on their accreditation, will be
developed so that individual institutions are not adversely
affected. This will empower private HEIs to set fees for their
programmes independently, though within the laid-out
norms and the broad applicable regulatory mechanism.
Private HEIs will be encouraged to offer freeships and
scholarships in significant numbers to their students. All fees
and charges set by private HEIs will be transparently and
fully disclosed, and there shall be no arbitrary increases in
these fees/charges during the period of enrolment of any
student. This fee determining mechanism will ensure

20
reasonable recovery of cost while ensuring that HEIs
discharge their social obligations."10
 (emphasis supplied)
26. It is noteworthy that NEP-2020 articulates a commitment to ensure
that there is no arbitrariness in the increase of fees in respect of
professional courses. It also contains a clear articulation of a policy
position against unjustified increases in the fee during a period of students'
enrolment.
27. The real question is whether the institutions and regulatory
committees entrusted with this responsibility are discharging their
functions efficiently and within a timeframe that gives meaningful certainty
to students, parents, and educational institutions alike.
28. The fee fixation committees established pursuant to this Court's
direction in Islamic Academy and PA Inamdar are discharging an
important function. It is necessary for the High Courts to ensure that these
bodies are in a position to effectively and efficiently perform their
obligations, as their recommendations have a direct bearing on the
aspiring students' access to higher educational opportunities and the
participating private enterprises' interest in establishing world-class
institutions. In the context of the compelling need to institutionalize the

functioning of such bodies and the important role which High Courts
exercise in ensuring that these bodies function effectively, this Court in
Lifecare Innovations Pvt. Ltd. and Another v. Union of India and Others11
held:
"22. While exercising judicial review of administrative action
in the context of Statutes, laws, rules or policies establishing
statutory or administrative bodies to implement the
provisions of the Act or its policy, the first duty of
constitutional courts is to ensure that these bodies are in a
position to effectively and efficiently perform their
obligations. This approach towards judicial review has
multiple advantages. In the first place, while continually
operating in the field with domain experts, these bodies
acquire domain expertise, the consequence of which would
also be informed decision-making and consistency. Further,
the critical mass of institutional memory acquired by these
bodies will have a direct bearing on the systematic
development of the sector and this will also help handling
polycentric issues. Thirdly, while continuously being on the
field, and having acquired the capability of making real-time
assessments about the working of the policies, these bodies
will be in a position to visualize course correction for future
policymaking.
23. Shifting the focus of judicial review to functional
capability of these bodies is not to be understood as an
argument for alternative remedy, much less as a suggestion
for judicial restraint. In fact, this shift is in recognition of an
important feature of judicial review, which performs the vital
role of institutionalizing authorities and bodies impressed
with statutory duties, ensuring they function effectively and
efficiently. The power of judicial review in matters
concerning implementation of policy objectives should
transcend the standard power of judicial review to issue
writs to perform statutory duty and proceed to examine
whether the duty bearers, the authorities and bodies
constituted properly and also whether they are functioning
effectively and efficiently. By ensuring institutional integrity
we achieve our institutional objectives. Further, effective

unnecessary litigation."
29. Institutional efficiency is not a matter of administrative convenience.
It is an essential component of fair and effective regulation. Certainty for
the students, sustainability for the institution, and efficiency in the
regulatory process are not competing objectives; they are complementary
elements of a sound system of professional education. The question,
therefore, is not whether a fee revision can take place, but the method and
manner in which it is undertaken, concluded, and put into effect.
30. A conjoint reading of Regulations 7(1), 7(4), and 7(5) of the AICTE
Regulations 1994 makes it clear that: (a) a revision of fees is permissible
only through the recommendation of the Committee, (b) it can be revised
only with a minimum gap of 3 years from the date of revision, (c) the
revision can only be on the recommendations based on estimated
expenditure of the professional colleges for efficient functioning, and (d)
while calculating the fees, the estimates of recurring expenditure shall be
based on at least the last two years audited figures of recurring
expenditure of the college and projected requirement of next three years.
31. Revised fees represent the cost of education determined at the
relevant point of time. If such cost is not recovered from the students at
the relevant time and is deferred to future batches, an inevitable revenue
deficit would certainly arise and will either have a cascading effect on

23
future batches or adversely affect the economic viability of the institution.
It will have its own fallout on the infrastructure, quality of lecturers and
professors, and also adversely affect student welfare. It is therefore
necessary to have periodic and effective revision of the fee payable as per
the regulations. In undertaking such revision, it is also necessary to adopt
and apply the principle of certainty with respect to the fees payable for the
professional course into which the student is admitted. This normative
principle is recognised in the AICTE Regulations 1994.
32. Institutional efficiency compels fee fixation committees to make
recommendations well in advance and the competent authorities to take
decisions well before the commencement of the admission process. The
committee should examine the relevant costs, including infrastructure,
faculty remuneration, maintenance, technology, statutory requirements,
and other legitimate expenditure, make a reasonable assessment of
foreseeable increases in such costs over the duration of the course, and
make recommendations so that the competent authorities take the
decision before the commencement of the course. A student entering a
four-or five-year professional programme should ordinarily know, at the
very threshold, the financial liability that they or their family is undertaking.
Such advance determination promotes transparency, enables informed
choice, and facilitates financial planning. This does not mean that the fee

24
structure must remain incapable of adjustment in every conceivable
circumstance. Costs may increase unexpectedly because of extraordinary
economic conditions, statutory changes or other circumstances which
could not reasonably have been anticipated. A narrowly defined
mechanism may therefore be provided to accommodate such exceptional
circumstances. But such adjustment must remain an exception and
cannot become a substitute for timely assessment and proper institutional
planning.
33. The larger principle is thus one of certainty through efficient
regulation. The fee fixation committees must function as continuing
institutions, capable of anticipating costs, undertaking periodic
assessments, and making timely decisions. Its processes should be
structured so that the fee determination is completed before admissions
commence and, as far as reasonably possible, covers the entire duration
of the professional course.
34. We may advert to the facts of the cases in hand. The fee for
professional courses in West Bengal was last revised in the 2016-17 AY.
The fee fixation committee and the State Government acted inefficiently
inasmuch as they failed to ensure the completion of revision exercise in
time for 2023-27 courses. A fresh revision of fee was undertaken after
seven years vide notification dated 16.10.2023. The Appellant-College

25
adopted the revised fee on 15.12.2023. The Appellant-College cannot be
blamed for its anxiety in implementing the revised fee structure after
conclusion of the first semester. The problem arising out of mid-stream
implementation of revised fee schedule could have been avoided, if the
State Government had issued the notification dated 16.10.2023 before the
commencement of academic session 2023-2024. We can take judicial
notice of the fact that functioning of the fee fixation committees as of now
and the State's action on their recommendations have often not been up
to the mark. The instant case demonstrates such one case.
35. While we uphold the conclusions drawn by the Division Bench of the
High Court for the independent reasons that we have given, we are not in
agreement with the reasoning of the Division Bench that the
implementation of the revised fee structure for the 2023-27 course will
have the effect of giving retrospective obligation to the Notification dated
16.10.2023. We are also of the opinion that the approach adopted by the
High Court in applying principles of equity and estoppel against the
Appellant-College on the basis of its admission brochure is not
sustainable in law. To that extent, the judgment of the High Court is set
aside.
36. For the reasons stated above, we partly allow Civil Appeals arising
out of SLP (C) No. 13237, 13690-13691, 16753, 14913-14914, 15617-

15618 and 16677 of 2026, against the judgment and order of the High
Court in Writ Appeal MAT Nos. 268, 288, 284 of 2026, and direct that;
(i) The fee fixation committees have a statutory foundation and have
an important public purpose to subserve. The institutionalisation of
these committees is necessary for realising the interests of aspiring
students for professional higher education and also for establishing
credible higher and professional educational institutions through
private enterprise. High Courts will exercise due judicial review to
ensure that these committees perform their duties with institutional
efficiency, expertise, and integrity.
(ii) The regulatory regime for fixation of fees, as contemplated in the
decisions of this Court, AICTE Regulations, National Education
Policy, 2020, coupled with principles of certainty, necessitates the
relevant authorities to notify fee payable for the entire course before
a student takes admission. There must be certainty about the fee
liability; variation in the fee payable during the subsistence of the
course is permissible only in exceptional instances such as
unforeseen increase in the expenditure.
(iii) The final directions of the High Court, as reproduced in
paragraph 15 of this judgment with respect to applicability of the
revised fees under Notification dated 16.10.2023 are affirmed. The
